title: Songs and Stories
label: ch:ml-arts
canDo: I can name a song, singing, dance and a story.

payoff.summary: From cold: the four arts words, and the three different things an ending does to the word in front of it.
payoff.note: Four atoms. THE EXAM POINT'S NOTE WAS ALREADY STALE WHEN THIS CHAPTER STARTED, the second such note in a row: it said 'nothing taught' of the arts, but chapter 98 gave the learner sinima, which is LEX-47's cinema limb. Checked before drafting rather than after, and the note is corrected rather than quietly replaced. NO NEW GRAMMAR, BY DESIGN. The three nouns were chosen so that each exercises a DIFFERENT one of the three aaNu outcomes the learner already owns, and none asks for a rule that has not been stated: paattu ends in the half-u and gives a sound up (ML-C69-words, and chapter 98's own newest rule, which until now had no fresh word to land on); nrttham ends in the anusvara and re-spells its m (ML-C89, ML-C96, ML-C97); katha ends in A and takes the ya glide, exactly as sinima does. Given up, re-spelled, added -- three events, and what tells them apart is only how the word ended. TWO INVENTIONS WERE CAUGHT BEFORE THE FIRST COMMIT, both by checking the corpus rather than trusting the draft. The dance example sentence read 'ithu sundaramaaya nrtthamaaNu', and sundaramaaya is attested NOWHERE -- an attributive form the book has never taught, the same trap that kept vrtthiketta out of chapter 97. It is now 'ithu nalla nrtthamaaNu', using the attributive nalla that ML-C98-sinima already models. And the romanization was written nr-with-ring-below; the track romanizes the vocalic r as r-with-dot-below in four independent witnesses (suhRttu, hRdayam, vRScikam, kRtajnjata), so it is nRtthaM. THE RECALL'S GRAMMAR LENS TABLE WAS DRAFTED FOUR COLUMNS WIDE and narrowed to three before any test ran -- chapter 98 shipped that defect and only the corpus-wide narration refusal count caught it, which would have left an audio learner a placeholder where the evidence belongs. The paattu/paaduka pair states a relation between TWO NAMED WORDS and explicitly refuses to generalise it: the noun's doubled TT thins to a single T in the verb, and the lesson says in as many words not to look for that in every noun beside a verb, because kali/kalikkuka does not do it. LITERATURE IS CLOSED ON katha, a concrete story word, rather than on saahityam, which is abstract and would need kavitha or a genre word beside it to be worth anything at A1.
